section.title: Paul's Ministry Among Them
section.sectionRationale: Against critics who questioned his motives, Paul defends the integrity of his ministry in Thessalonica: bold in God, free of flattery and greed, gentle as a nursing mother and firm as a father, working night and day so as not to burden anyone. He then thanks God that they received his message as the word of God, and that they, like the churches in Judea, suffered for it.
section.thesis: True gospel ministry is entrusted by God and answers to God, marked by boldness, purity of motive, tender and fatherly love, and self-giving labor; and the word so preached is received as the very word of God, which then works in believers even through suffering.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the purity of Paul's motives and manner; the tenderness and toil of his fatherly, motherly care; and thanksgiving that they received the word of God and shared in the churches' suffering.

units.label: A ministry of pure motives
units.note: entrusted by God, not pleasing men

verses.text: You yourselves know, brothers, that our visit to you was not in vain.
As you are aware, we had already endured suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi. But in the face of strong opposition, we were bold in our God to speak to you the {{euangelion|gospel}} of God.
For our appeal does not arise from deceit or ulterior motives or trickery.
Instead, we speak as those {{dokimazo|approved}} by God to be entrusted with the gospel, not in order to please men but God, who examines our hearts.
As you know, we never used words of flattery or any pretext for {{pleonexia|greed}}. God is our witness!
Nor did we seek praise from you or from anyone else, although as {{apostolos|apostles}} of Christ we had authority to demand it.

units.label: A ministry of tenderness and toil
units.note: like a nursing mother, like a father

verses.text: On the contrary, we were gentle among you, like a nursing {{trophos|mother}} caring for her children.
We cared so deeply that we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well. That is how beloved you have become to us.
Surely you recall, brothers, our labor and toil. We worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.
You are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous, and blameless our conduct was among you who believed.
For you know that we treated each of you as a father treats his own children,
encouraging you, comforting you, and urging you to walk in a manner {{axios|worthy}} of God, who {{kaleo|calls}} you into His own {{basileia|kingdom}} and glory.

units.label: The word received, the suffering shared
units.note: the word of God at work in believers

verses.text: And we continually thank God because, when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the {{logos|word}} of God, which is also now at {{energeo|work}} in you who believe.
For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Judea that are in Christ Jesus. You suffered from your own countrymen the very things they suffered from the Jews,
who killed both the Lord Jesus and their own prophets and drove us out as well. They are displeasing to God and hostile to all men,
hindering us from telling the Gentiles how they may be saved. As a result, they continue to heap up their sins to full capacity; the utmost {{orge|wrath}} has come upon them.

euangelion.gloss: The gospel, the good news of God. Paul repeatedly calls it the gospel of God, stressing that it originates with God and belongs to Him, not to the preacher. He was entrusted with it and answers to God for how he handles it. This governs the whole defense of his ministry.

dokimazo.gloss: To test, examine, and so approve after testing. Paul says he was approved by God, tested and found fit to be entrusted with the gospel, and that God examines his heart. The same word runs beneath the passage: the God who tests the messenger is the one he seeks to please, not men.

pleonexia.gloss: Greed, covetousness, the grasping desire for more. Paul insists he never used ministry as a pretext for greed, a common charge against traveling teachers. His refusal to exploit the Thessalonians for gain is part of proving that his message came from pure, God-approved motives.

apostolos.gloss: An apostle, one sent with the authority of the sender. Paul notes that as apostles of Christ he and his companions could have made demands, yet they laid that right aside. The word underlines both his genuine authority and his deliberate gentleness in not pressing it.

trophos.gloss: A nurse or nursing mother. Paul pictures his gentleness among them as a mother tenderly caring for her own children. It is one of Scripture's most tender images of pastoral care, set beside the father image in verse 11 to capture both nurture and formative guidance.

axios.gloss: Worthily, in a manner that fits or matches. Paul urged them to walk worthy of God, to live in a way that matches the God who called them. It is the goal of his fatherly exhortation: not bare rule-keeping but a life that corresponds to the greatness of the God who saves.

kaleo.gloss: To call or summon. God is the one who calls believers into His own kingdom and glory. The call is effective and gracious, and it defines the Christian's destiny. Paul returns to God as the faithful caller at the letter's close, assuring them the One who calls will also keep them.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, the reign and realm of God. Believers are called into God's own kingdom and glory, their sure destiny in Christ. The word lifts the readers' eyes from present suffering to the coming reign they will share, giving weight to Paul's plea that they walk worthy of it.

logos.gloss: Word, message, or account. Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians received his preaching not as the word of men but as what it truly is, the word of God. The term carries the conviction that in the apostolic gospel God Himself speaks, so the message has divine authority and power.

energeo.gloss: To work, be active, produce an effect. The word of God is now at work in those who believe, energizing and transforming them. The same root gives us energy. Paul's point is that the received word is not inert information but an active, effective power operating within believers.

orge.gloss: Wrath, God's righteous judgment against sin. Paul says the utmost wrath has come upon those who oppose the gospel and hinder the salvation of the Gentiles. It is the sober counterpart to the salvation being offered, and a reminder that persistent opposition to God's saving purpose meets His just judgment.

basic.context: Paul had to leave Thessalonica suddenly, and critics apparently began to slander him, suggesting he was just another traveling con man in it for money and praise. Here he reminds the church what his time among them was actually like: bold, honest, gentle, hardworking, and self-sacrificing. Then he gives thanks that they received his message as God's own word and, like other churches, suffered for it.
basic.hermeneutics: This is partly a defense of Paul's ministry and partly a model of what gospel ministry should look like. We should read it both as Paul answering real accusations and as a lasting pattern: those who handle God's word must do so with pure motives, tenderness, and integrity, aiming to please God rather than people.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul preaches the euangelion, gospel, of God, having been dokimazo, approved and entrusted with it. He rejects pleonexia, greed, and though an apostolos, apostle, with authority, he was gentle as a trophos, nursing mother. He urged them to walk axios, worthy, of the God who kaleo, calls, them into His basileia, kingdom. They received the logos, word, of God, which now energeo, works, in them.
basic.typology: Paul as a suffering messenger stands in the line of the prophets, who were killed by their own people, and points to Christ, the rejected messenger who was killed yet vindicated. The word of God at work in believers echoes God's word that always accomplishes what He sends it to do.
basic.christ: The gospel Paul carries is the good news of Christ, who died and rose. He notes that the Lord Jesus was killed, sharing the fate of the prophets and of His messengers. The kingdom and glory believers are called into are Christ's, and the salvation being offered to the Gentiles is salvation through Him.
basic.god: This is the gospel of God, entrusted by God, aimed at pleasing God, who examines hearts and calls people into His own kingdom and glory. God is the one at work through His word in believers. He is also just: persistent opposition to His saving purpose meets His righteous wrath.
basic.crossReferences: Second Corinthians 4 describes the same refusal to tamper with God's word for gain. Acts 17 recounts the opposition Paul faced in Thessalonica. And Isaiah 55 promises that God's word does not return empty but accomplishes His purpose.
basic.oneStory: God has always sent messengers with His word, and His people have often suffered for receiving it, from the prophets to the Lord Jesus to the young churches. Paul's ministry is one link in that chain: the word of God, faithfully carried and joyfully received, now at work in a suffering church being called into God's kingdom.

context.literary:
This section is built on memory. Again and again in verses 1 to 12 Paul appeals to what the readers already know, with phrases such as 'you yourselves know,' 'as you are aware,' 'you recall,' and 'you are witnesses.' He is not teaching new truth. He is calling the church itself into the witness box, and twice he adds a second and higher witness: 'God is our witness' in verse 5 and 'so is God' in verse 10. A defence of this kind is much stronger when the hearers can confirm it from their own experience.

The section moves in three steps, each with its own image. In verses 1 to 6 the negative side is set out in a run of denials: not deceit, not ulterior motives, not trickery, not flattery, not greed, not a search for praise. In verses 7 to 12 two pictures give the positive side, first a gentle mother and then an exhorting father, with the heavy labour of verse 9 placed between them as the proof of both. The third step, verses 13 to 16, appears to change the subject, from the preachers to the hearers, but it is the same argument turned around. If the messengers were honest, then the word that came through them was what it claimed to be, and the Thessalonians' suffering fits the pattern of all who receive it.

Within the letter, the chapter explains why Paul can write with such confidence in chapters 4 and 5. A man who has lived this way earns the right to give the instructions that follow.
context.historical:
Roving teachers and orators were a familiar sight in the Greek cities of the first century. Some were serious philosophers; others charged fees, courted rich patrons, flattered crowds, and moved on when the money ran out. When Paul left Thessalonica after a short stay, Acts 17:10, it was easy for opponents to tar him with the same brush and say that he had fled with whatever he could take. The long list of denials in verses 3 to 6 reads like a reply to just such a charge. Paul did not set up as a professional lecturer. He worked at a trade, Acts 18:3, and says here that he worked night and day so as not to be a burden, verse 9. Philippians 4:16 adds that the Philippians sent help to him more than once while he was in Thessalonica, which shows that his own labour was not enough to sustain him and that he still declined to demand support from the converts.

The shameful treatment at Philippi is told in Acts 16:19 to 24, where Paul and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods, and put in the inner cell. Having just been publicly shamed, they went on to Thessalonica and preached boldly. Verses 14 to 16 reflect the harassment recorded in Acts 17:5 to 9, and the 'churches of God in Judea' had met their own hostility, Acts 8:1, 12:1 to 3, and Galatians 1:22. The remark in verse 15 about the prophets killed by their own people echoes a tradition found in the Old Testament and the teaching of Jesus, 1 Kings 19:10, 2 Chronicles 36:15 and 16, and Matthew 23:31 to 37.
context.canonical:
The passage gives the New Testament one of its fullest portraits of a model minister, and several of its lines are echoed elsewhere. Paul tells the Corinthians that he does not peddle God's word for profit, 2 Corinthians 2:17 and 4:2, and that he refused support from them so as not to hinder the gospel, 1 Corinthians 9:12 and 15. Peter's charge to elders in 1 Peter 5:2 and 3 speaks in the same breath of not serving for sordid gain and not lording it over the flock. The picture of a pastor as a parent shows up in 1 Corinthians 4:14 to 16, Galatians 4:19, and Philemon 10.

The affirmation of verse 13 stands beside 2 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Peter 1:20 and 21 as a New Testament witness to the apostolic message as God's own word. The claim that this word 'is now at work' in believers recalls Isaiah 55:10 and 11 and Hebrews 4:12.

The sharp verses 14 to 16 belong to a long line of prophetic denunciation, in which a prophet who is himself of the people declares judgment on its leaders. They should be read alongside Stephen's speech in Acts 7:51 to 53 and Jesus' words in Matthew 23, and set against Romans 9 to 11, where the same author insists that God has not rejected His people and that all Israel will be saved, Romans 11:1 and 26.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Paul writes to strengthen a church whose confidence in its founders was being shaken. If the men who brought the message were frauds, then the message itself, and everything the Thessalonians had given up for it, was in doubt. So he reminds them of what they saw with their own eyes: men who risked their lives, worked with their hands, and treated them like family. He does not mean this as boasting. He means it as a defence of the gospel's credibility. At the same time he is giving them, and every later servant of the word, a standard to measure by. He then turns to the thing that matters most to him, that they received the word for what it is, and that their suffering for it places them in a long and honourable company. His aim is a church that does not wobble when slander arrives, because it knows what it received and from whom.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Most of the passage is description of what Paul and his team did. It is not a rule that every minister must work a trade, or that no church may support its teachers. Paul himself defends the right to support in 1 Corinthians 9:3 to 14, and here he says he had the authority to make demands, verse 6. What carries over is the spirit: no manipulation, no hunger for money or praise, tenderness joined to firmness, and a willingness to share one's own life. The comment about opponents in verses 15 and 16 is also description of a particular conflict in the first century, not a command about how to treat any people today. Reading it as a charge against all Jews, then or now, would contradict the same author's grief and love for his own people in Romans 9:1 to 5. The word of God accepted 'as the true word of God' in verse 13 is a statement of what happened and an invitation to receive the apostolic word the same way.

debates.question: Who are 'the Jews' of verses 14 to 16, and is the passage hostile to the Jewish people?

views.label: Particular opponents, described by a Jewish apostle
views.case: Paul is himself a Jew and writes to a church made up largely of Gentiles. His own account of these verses is that Judean opponents drove out the preachers and hindered the Gentile mission. Many readers hold that he is naming specific persecutors in Judea and Thessalonica, in the manner of the prophets, and not condemning a nation. They point to Romans 9:1 to 5 and 11:1, where he says he would be cut off for his kin.

views.label: A later addition to the letter
views.case: A number of scholars have proposed that verses 15 and 16 were added after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, since they seem to say that the wrath has already come. They note how harsh the language is. Other scholars reply that no manuscript omits the lines and that Paul's style can be sharp when he is hurt.

views.label: A prophetic judgment on those who resist the gospel
views.case: Others read the passage as the language of a prophet who stands within his people. The charge of killing the prophets is familiar, and the rebuke is for those who stand in the way of the gospel for the Gentiles, not for Jews as such.

debates.bearing: Every responsible reading agrees that these verses cannot support contempt for Jewish people today. Paul counts himself within Israel, and the surrounding letter and Romans 11 make clear that God has not abandoned them.

debates.question: What does it mean that 'the utmost wrath has come upon them'?

views.label: The judgment of AD 70
views.case: Some link the wrath to the fall of Jerusalem and the Temple, which Jesus foretold in Luke 19:41 to 44 and 21:20 to 24. On this view, if the letter is early, Paul is speaking prophetically of what is certain to come.

views.label: A settled spiritual judgment already in motion
views.case: Others hold that the tense speaks of God's judicial hardening, in the way Romans 1:18 to 32 describes wrath as already operating against sin. The 'filling up' of sins matches a pattern from Genesis 15:16 and Matthew 23:32, where God waits until measure is full.

views.label: The final wrath of the last day
views.case: A third view sees the final wrath at the end of the age, which Paul has already named in 1:10 and develops in 5:9. Wrath 'has come' in the sense that its arrival is certain.

debates.bearing: The first two views see wrath arriving within history, and the third at the end, but all three insist that God's judgment is real and consistent. None of them gives the Thessalonians any reason for revenge. The rebuke is meant to explain suffering and to warn, and the very gospel that the opponents hindered is still offered, verse 16.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words in this passage show how careful Paul is about the kind of speaker he is. In verse 2 'we were bold' translates a verb, parrhesiazomai, that grows from parrhesia, the free speech of a citizen who says what he thinks and fears no one. It was a prized quality in Greek public life, and Paul claims it for the gospel, not for himself: bold 'in our God.' The word 'appeal' in verse 3 is paraklesis, which can mean exhortation, comfort, or encouragement depending on context, and Paul will use its verb in verse 11 and again in 4:1. A paraklesis is neither a lecture nor a performance but a calling alongside.

In verse 5 the word translated 'flattery' is kolakeia, the cultivated charm of a person who tells others what they want to hear so as to gain something. Paired with 'pretext' (prophasis), which means an excuse that hides the real reason, it shows that Paul can name both the technique and the motive. He calls on God, not the Thessalonians, as witness to the motive, since no human can see a heart.

In verse 7 there is a well known textual choice. Some Greek manuscripts read 'gentle' (epioi) and others read 'infants' (nepioi), which would give 'we were infants among you, like a nursing mother.' The reading 'gentle' is preferred by most editors and is the one in the Berean Standard Bible, though the other has ancient support. Both fit the image of tenderness, and the difference is a single letter.

Verse 8 uses a word for 'lives', psychai, usually translated 'souls', so that the phrase is literally to share 'our own souls.' It means the whole person, not just the message. Verse 9 pairs two words for toil, kopos and mochthos, 'labour and hardship', which Paul also uses together in 2 Thessalonians 3:8 and 2 Corinthians 11:27, and which suggest exhausting physical work.

In verse 13, Paul says they 'received' (paralambano) the word from him and then 'accepted' (dechomai) it. The first verb is the one used for handing on a trust from one person to another; the second is the verb of welcome. The word came as a tradition passed down, but it was welcomed as a message from God.

In verse 16 the phrase 'to heap up their sins to full capacity' translates a verb, anaplerosai, meaning to fill up. The picture is of a measure being filled, and the 'full capacity' is God's measure, not man's.

typology.type: The prophet rejected by his own people, 1 Thessalonians 2:15
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah was beaten and put in stocks, Jeremiah 20:1 and 2, and Elijah felt alone with the prophets killed, 1 Kings 19:10. Paul places himself and his companions in this line, and puts Jesus as the climactic case: the Lord Jesus was killed, and so were the prophets before Him. In Christ the pattern reaches its centre. The rejected messenger is the Son Himself, Matthew 21:33 to 39, and His rejection becomes the means of rescue. The type falls short because the prophets died as witnesses to a rescue they could only announce, while Christ's death accomplished it.

typology.type: The leader who feels like a nurse, 1 Thessalonians 2:7
typology.fulfillment: Moses once cried out that he could not carry the people like a nurse carries a baby, Numbers 11:12. Paul claims for himself the very role that Moses found impossible, and he does it through the strength God supplies, as 2 Corinthians 3:5 and 6 explains. In Christ the picture is perfected. He longs to gather Jerusalem 'as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings,' Matthew 23:37, and Isaiah 66:13 shows that tenderness is not foreign to the Father. The type falls short because Moses and Paul tire and fail; the Lord's care does not.

typology.type: The word that accomplishes its purpose, 1 Thessalonians 2:13
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 55:10 and 11 compares God's word to rain that does not return without watering the earth, and says it will not return empty. Paul sees this at work in a church that did not exist a year before. In Christ the word takes flesh, John 1:1 and 14, and Hebrews 4:12 calls it living and active. The type falls short because Isaiah describes a word of God that goes out in speech; the gospel is the word that is also a Person who will return.

At Sinai God called Israel to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, Exodus 19:6. Paul applies the call to a mixed church of Gentile believers, in the present tense of the verb 'calls.' Peter does the same in 1 Peter 2:9. In Christ the kingdom is no longer a national hope tied to one land but the reign of the risen King, shared with those who belong to Him, Revelation 1:6. The type falls short because Israel's kingdom was always partial and could be lost; the kingdom of Christ is entered by call and kept by His power.

study.christ:
The passage names Christ on its surface only a few times, but the whole defence rests on His pattern. The apostles are 'apostles of Christ' in verse 6 and speak 'by the authority' of the one who sent them, the same authority Paul invokes in 4:2. They are tender because He is tender, and they work and suffer because He did.

The most striking Christological statement is in verse 15, where Paul says the Lord Jesus was killed. It stands in a sentence about the prophets and about the apostles, so the cross is placed in a line of rejected messengers, yet Jesus is not just the last in the list. He is called 'the Lord Jesus', and the same title is used throughout the letter for the one who will return. The one who was killed is the one who will come, 1:10. Paul does not mention the resurrection here, but the whole letter assumes it.

The gospel is called 'the gospel of God' in verses 2, 8, and 9, and elsewhere 'the gospel of Christ', 3:2. The two titles are not rivals. The gospel comes from God and is about Christ, and Paul can give either name without feeling any difference. The kingdom of verse 12 is likewise God's, but in the other letters it belongs to the Son, Colossians 1:13.

There is an important pattern of imitation. In 1:6 the Thessalonians imitated the apostles and the Lord, and here in verse 14 they imitate the churches in Judea 'that are in Christ Jesus.' The phrase 'in Christ Jesus' shows that the believers of Thessalonica and those in Judea share one life despite the distance and differences of language and culture.

We should not make Christ appear where the text does not: the nursing mother is not an image of Jesus, and the labour of Paul is not an allegory of the cross. But the passage gives the reader a very concrete picture of what the Lord's ministry looks like when it is carried by His servants, and Matthew 23:37 and Philippians 2:5 to 8 show that the picture comes from Him.
study.god:
This passage insists on a God who sees what no one else can. Three times Paul sets God against human observers: God 'examines our hearts' in verse 4, 'God is our witness' in verse 5, and God joins the Thessalonians as a witness in verse 10. The point is not that the readers are unreliable, but that motives are hidden from every eye but one. For a servant of the word that is both a pressure and a freedom. It removes any reason to perform for others, and it removes any hope of hiding behind appearances. The same truth is in Jeremiah 17:10 and 1 Samuel 16:7.

God is the one who 'entrusts' the gospel. The word in verse 4 is one used for a treasure placed in someone's care, which implies that the gospel is not Paul's to edit or improve. The God who tests the messenger also gives the message. And the message is the gospel 'of God', so that the Giver and the content cannot be separated.

God also 'calls' into His own kingdom and glory, verse 12. Paul's verb is in the present tense, which suggests that the call is ongoing as well as accomplished. The call has a destination, the glory that Christ shares, and a present consequence, a manner of life that is 'worthy' of the One who calls. God does not just invite from a distance. He names, brings, and then leads His people.

The word itself is alive with God's activity. Verse 13 says it 'is now at work' in believers. The One who spoke creation into being does not step away from what He has said. Preaching is therefore not mere information; it is the vehicle of a living God.

The passage also holds together tenderness and justice. The Father who is imaged by a mother and father in verses 7 to 11 is the same God whose wrath comes upon persistent opposition in verse 16. Paul does not feel the need to reconcile the two by softening either. For worship, the passage invites reverence before a God who sees the heart, gratitude for the word received, and confidence that He finishes what He calls.

crossReferences.note: The beating and imprisonment at Philippi that Paul calls 'shameful treatment' in verse 2. The scene shows what 'in the face of strong opposition' meant: Paul and Silas had been publicly stripped and flogged only days before they preached in Thessalonica.

Luke's account of the same visit from the outside. His three Sabbaths and Paul's departure by night explain why the apostle's absence became fertile soil for slander, and why he insists the visit was 'not in vain.'

Paul says that, unlike many, he does not peddle the word of God for profit but speaks with sincerity as from God. The same distinction runs through 1 Thessalonians 2:3 to 5, which shows that this was Paul's regular contrast with the travelling salesmen of the day.

Paul argues that he has the right to support but does not use it, so as not to hinder the gospel. It helps explain 'we had authority to demand it' in verse 6 and shows that his refusal was a policy chosen out of love.

The Philippians twice sent aid when Paul was in Thessalonica. It fills in the background of verse 9: his labour did not mean he was alone, and the giving of a friendly church did not compromise his independence.

Moses complains that he cannot carry the people like a nurse carries an infant. Paul's image of a nursing mother in verse 7 shows an apostle willing to do what Moses felt crushed by, and he does it by giving 'our own lives as well.'

Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chicks, and says the city kills the prophets. The two thoughts in this verse sit side by side in 1 Thessalonians 2:7 and 15, which suggests Paul had absorbed the Lord's own feeling for his people.
God's word goes out like rain and does not return empty. It is the background to 'now at work in you who believe' in verse 13, and it explains why a church could be formed in a few weeks.

Paul asks whether God has rejected His people and answers no, since he is himself an Israelite. It guards the reading of verses 14 to 16 against any suggestion that the apostle wished judgment on his own nation as such.

God tells Abraham the sin of the Amorites is not yet complete. The idea of a measure being filled before judgment falls is the background to 'heap up their sins to full capacity' in verse 16, and it shows that God's patience has a limit.

study.oneStory:
From Genesis onward God speaks and sends people to speak for Him, and the story of the Old Testament is how often His messengers were resisted. Abel was killed, Noah mocked, Moses doubted, and the prophets beaten, stoned, and sawn in two, as the roll call of Hebrews 11:36 to 38 recalls. This passage places the apostolic mission in that same long line. The preachers in Thessalonica suffer as the prophets did, and the Thessalonian converts suffer as the churches of Judea did.

Yet the story is not only about rejection. It is also about a word that works. From 'let there be light' in Genesis 1:3 to the promise of Isaiah 55:11, God's speech does what it says. In Thessalonica a handful of Greeks are made a people by a word received in a few weeks, which is the same creating power at work in a new place.

The passage also looks ahead. The 'kingdom and glory' in verse 12 are the destination of the whole biblical story, when the reign of God is finally seen in a renewed world. The 'wrath' in verse 16 belongs to the same horizon, since God's judgment on stubborn opposition is part of how that kingdom comes. In the new creation the tenderness of the nursing mother and the firmness of the father, which Paul put into his own ministry, will no longer need to be borrowed. Revelation 21:3 and 4 pictures God Himself wiping every tear, and the nations that were once hindered from hearing will be among those who walk in His light, Revelation 21:24. What began in a few weeks of work in a Macedonian marketplace ends in a city whose gates never close.

sermon.title: Ministry Like a Nursing Mother: 1 Thessalonians 2:5-8, Part 6
sermon.why: Piper examines how Paul could be gentle as a nursing mother and yet firm as an exhorting father, drawing out the pure motives and self-giving love that mark true gospel ministry in this movement.

quiz.q: What was Paul's aim in his preaching, according to verse 4?

options.text: To please God, who examines hearts, not to please men.
options.note: Verse 4 makes pleasing God, not men, the governing aim.

options.text: To please as many people as possible.
options.note: Paul explicitly denies aiming to please men; he aimed to please God.

options.text: To build a personal following and reputation.
options.note: He refused to seek praise from anyone; his aim was God's approval.

options.text: To make as much money as he could.
options.note: Paul denies any greed and worked night and day to avoid burdening them.

quiz.q: Which two family images does Paul use for his ministry among them?

options.text: A nursing mother caring for her children and a father exhorting his children.
options.note: Verses 7 and 11 give the mother and father images.

options.text: A stern judge and a distant king.
options.note: Paul had authority but chose tenderness, not stern distance.

options.text: A hired servant and a business partner.
options.note: The images are familial and loving, not commercial.

options.text: A soldier and a tax collector.
options.note: Paul uses gentle family imagery, mother and father.

quiz.q: How did the Thessalonians receive Paul's message, and why does it matter?

options.text: Not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the word of God, which works in them.
options.note: Verse 13 states they received it as God's word, now at work in believers.

options.text: As interesting human opinions to consider.
options.note: They received it as God's word, not merely human opinion.

options.text: As one option among many equally valid views.
options.note: They accepted it as the authoritative word of God, not one option among many.

options.text: As a message they could safely ignore.
options.note: They embraced it as God's word, which is actively at work in them.

quiz.q: Why did Paul work night and day while he was among them?

options.text: So as not to be a burden to anyone while he preached the gospel.
options.note: Verse 9 gives this reason for his labor and toil.

options.text: Because he enjoyed the money more than preaching.
options.note: He worked precisely so he would not seek gain from them.

options.text: Because the church forced him to earn his keep.
options.note: He chose this freely, out of love, to avoid burdening them.

options.text: Because he had no interest in the church.
options.note: He labored out of deep care, sharing his very life with them.

quiz.q: Into what does Paul say God calls believers?

options.text: Into His own kingdom and glory.
options.note: Verse 12 names God's kingdom and glory as the believers' calling.

options.text: Into a life of ease and comfort now.
options.note: The calling is to God's kingdom and glory, often reached through suffering.

options.text: Into strict rule-keeping for its own sake.
options.note: He calls them to walk worthy of God, not to bare legalism.

options.text: Into nothing in particular.
options.note: God calls them into a definite and glorious destiny, His kingdom and glory.

questions: Paul aimed to please God, who examines hearts, rather than to please people. Whose approval are you most tempted to live for, and how would seeking God's approval change things?
Paul combined a mother's tenderness with a father's exhortation. In caring for others, do you lean too far toward softness or toward hardness, and where do you need the balance Paul shows?
The Thessalonians received the message as the word of God, not the word of men. How does it change your Bible reading to expect God Himself to speak and to work in you through it?
Paul worked hard so as not to burden others and to keep his motives clear. Where might God be calling you to serve at cost to yourself so your love is unmistakable?
The word of God is at work in those who believe. Where have you seen God's word actually changing you, and where do you long for it to work more deeply?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts and editions attach the clause about apostolic authority to verse 7, reading that the apostles could have been a burden.
The BSB footnote records a variant, we were like young children among you, reflecting a difference of a single letter in the Greek behind gentle and infants.
The BSB footnote offers at last the wrath of God has come upon them as an alternative rendering of the closing clause.
